problems.form_value: what_was_assigned: 'Generating one idea with ChatGPT ('ChatGPT–human' ideas) or without aid ('Human-only')'. Arm 'ChatGPT–human' (ai generative_ai): 'Fig. 1 label, read as participants who worked with ChatGPT under the paper's statement that participants were randomized to work with or without ChatGPT'.
problems.source_says: c015 uses 'ChatGPT–human' only in Fig. 1 (panel title and bar label). It never says who produced these ideas or how they were assigned, and its text on study 2b names only the ChatGPT-only set and 'human ideas'. The arm coding is therefore an inference, which rule 1 of the form spec bars, and the form's open_questions concede the gap. The coding is right on the facts: Lee and Chung (c010) describe ChatGPT 'in collaboration with humans (the ChatGPT-assisted condition)' (PDF p. 3) and randomly assigned people only to that condition or Human-only (PDF p. 7). Fix: cite c010 as the basis for this arm, not as a cross-check.
problems.quote: Experiment 2b: human versus ChatGPT–human versus ChatGPT-only ideas
problems.locator: c015 p. 1108 (PDF p. 2), Fig. 1 panel title; c010 (Lee and Chung 2024) PDF p. 3 (journal p. 1908), Results, Experiment 2B, and PDF p. 7 (journal p. 1912), Methods, Experiment 2B

problems.field: studies[S1].arms[*].description; also S1-O1 diversity_detail.computed_over and the agreed field 'one idea per participant' (one idea equals one person)
problems.form_value: 'Participants who generated their idea with ChatGPT; one idea per participant; count not stated.' (same wording for Web-search-assisted); S1-O1 computed over 'All pairs of ideas within each condition's pool (one idea per participant)'
problems.source_says: c015 says 'Each participant submitted one idea' for the whole series (p. 1107). Lee and Chung's Methods say that in Experiment 1 participants could enter several ideas, about 1.69 on average, each scored separately, and the reconciled c010 form records this in its S1 task description. So 'one idea per participant' and 'one idea equals one person' are wrong for S1: its pool can hold more ideas than people, and pairs of ideas from the same person. c015 does not say how its analysis handled the extra ideas. Random, individual, between assignment is not affected (c010 PDF p. 6). Fix: state the conflict in the S1 arm descriptions instead of one idea per participant.
problems.quote: The participants could submit as many ideas as they liked, and there was no time limit on the task.
problems.locator: c010 (Lee and Chung 2024) PDF p. 6 (journal p. 1911), Methods, Experiment 1 (same page: 'The participants entered around 1.69 ideas on average'); c015 p. 1107 (PDF p. 1), left column, first paragraph

problems.form_value: other, because 'the document does not say whether the experiments ran online, in a lab, or in the field'
problems.source_says: The form spec's field note says that 'A reanalysis of another paper's experiment takes that experiment's design class'. c015 is such a reanalysis (its Reporting Summary calls it a secondary analysis of Lee and Chung's data). The reconciled c010 form codes all six Lee and Chung experiments online_rct, because Lee and Chung randomly assigned MTurk or Prolific participants in each. The value 'other' also conflicts with randomized 'yes' and eligibility core 'yes': the codebook gives the core role only to lab_rct, online_rct and field_rct. Fix: online_rct for S1 to S6, citing c010.
problems.quote: Secondary analysis of previously published data by Lee & Chung (2024)
problems.locator: c015 Reporting Summary, Behavioural & social sciences study design, Study description, PDF p. 5; form-spec.md, Field notes, design_class; c010.json, design_class of S1 to S6; c010 PDF p. 2 and pp. 6-8, Methods

problems.form_value: Participants were instructed to use ChatGPT while generating their idea; the interface and instructions are not described in this document.
problems.source_says: Minor. c015's general sentence says participants were instructed to use ChatGPT (p. 1107). In Experiment 2A, Lee and Chung gave permission, not an instruction: the ChatGPT arm was told it could use the ChatGPT website. Suggested wording: 'Participants were told they could use the ChatGPT website (Lee and Chung, c010, PDF p. 2); c015 does not describe the interface.'
problems.quote: Participants in the ChatGPT-assisted condition were told that they could use the ChatGPT website, while those in the Web-search-assisted condition were told that they could use the Google search engine.
problems.locator: c010 (Lee and Chung 2024) PDF p. 2 (journal p. 1907), Results, Experiment 2A; c015 p. 1107 (PDF p. 1), left column, first paragraph

confirmed.statement: c015 states random assignment once, for Lee and Chung's whole series, and the form's assignment quote is verbatim ('they randomized participants to complete various creative challenges, either with or without the help of ChatGPT'). There is no per-experiment statement, as the form's open_questions say.
confirmed.locator: c015 p. 1107 (PDF p. 1), left column, first paragraph

confirmed.statement: c015 itself randomized no one. Its Reporting Summary lists a secondary analysis of Lee and Chung's data with Randomization 'N/A', and Lee and Chung collected the data, so 'Lee and Chung (2024) did the randomization' is right.
confirmed.locator: c015 Reporting Summary, PDF p. 5; Data availability, p. 1109 (PDF p. 3)

confirmed.statement: In S1, S2, S4, S5 and S6 the assigned factor is use of ChatGPT for the participant's own idea, against web search or no aid. The scored outputs are the participants' own ideas, not conditions that differ only in whose output is evaluated.
confirmed.locator: c015 p. 1107 (PDF p. 1): 'instructing participants to use ChatGPT' and 'humans with and without web searches'; Fig. 1 arm labels, p. 1108 (PDF p. 2)

confirmed.statement: The tool is generative AI. c015 treats Lee and Chung's ChatGPT results as evidence on 'large language models in idea generation' and says 'generative AI benefits individual ideas'. c015 gives no model version (Lee and Chung used GPT-3.5).
confirmed.locator: c015 p. 1107 (PDF p. 1), first paragraph; p. 1108 (PDF p. 2), left column below Fig. 1; c010 PDF p. 1, abstract

confirmed.statement: Comparison arms match the Fig. 1 labels: S1 and S4 web search (other_aid); S2 Human (none) and web search (other_aid); S3 Human-only (none); S5 and S6 web search, titled Google, at each level of the second factor (other_aid). Lee and Chung's Human-only arms used no external web resources.
confirmed.locator: c015 p. 1108 (PDF p. 2), Fig. 1; p. 1107 (PDF p. 1), right column ('web-search-aided condition', 'human-only condition'); c010 PDF pp. 2 and 7

confirmed.statement: Unit individual and between structure are right for all six studies: Lee and Chung randomly assigned each participant to one condition, with 2 x 2 between-participants designs in Experiments 4 and 5. No study is within-person, so order randomization does not apply.
confirmed.locator: c015 p. 1107 (PDF p. 1); c010 PDF p. 2 (Experiment 2A), p. 6 (Experiment 1), p. 7 (Experiments 2B, 3 and 4), pp. 7-8 (Experiment 5)

confirmed.statement: The S3 ChatGPT-only set is AI output with no participant ('AI-generated ideas (ChatGPT-only)'). The form rightly keeps it out of the assigned arms and codes S3-O2 as ai_vs_human context. Lee and Chung got these 100 responses by entering the task prompt into ChatGPT-3.5 themselves.
confirmed.locator: c015 p. 1108 (PDF p. 2), right column, first paragraph; c010 PDF p. 7, Methods, Experiment 2B

confirmed.statement: S5 and S6: the form rightly says c015 does not describe how the constraint or empathy factor was assigned. Lee and Chung randomized all four cells, so the within-level ChatGPT versus web search contrasts are randomized.
confirmed.locator: c015 p. 1108 (PDF p. 2), Fig. 1 panels 'Experiment 4' and 'Experiment 5'; c010 PDF p. 7 (Experiment 4) and pp. 7-8 (Experiment 5), Methods

confirmed.statement: Reading c015's series-level sentence as covering every experiment is right: Lee and Chung state that in all experiments participants were randomly assigned to use or not use ChatGPT assistance.
confirmed.locator: c010 PDF p. 2 (journal p. 1907), paragraph before Results

confirmed.statement: ai_tool.role open_chat fits: c015 says participants were instructed to use ChatGPT, and Lee and Chung's ChatGPT arms used the ChatGPT website itself.
confirmed.locator: c015 p. 1107 (PDF p. 1); c010 PDF p. 2 (Experiment 2A) and PDF p. 7 (Experiment 2B, Methods)

confirmed.statement: Arm names in the form match the Fig. 1 text layer in every panel, including the Experiment 5 order Web search (base), Web search (high), ChatGPT (high), ChatGPT (base).

summary: c015, a secondary analysis, states random assignment once for Lee and Chung's whole series (p. 1107); with the Fig. 1 arm labels, that supports individual, between-participant assignment to ChatGPT versus web search or no aid in S1, S2, S4, S5 and S6, and Lee and Chung's Methods confirm it for all six experiments. The coding is still refuted in parts: c015 never defines the Experiment 2b 'ChatGPT–human' arm, the S1 arms repeat 'one idea per participant' although Lee and Chung report about 1.69 ideas each in Experiment 1, design_class 'other' breaks the form-spec rule that a reanalysis takes the original's class (online_rct), and the S2 how_used says 'instructed' where Experiment 2A only permitted ChatGPT use.
